units: the craftswoman answers her pupil's questions about the cloth kept in the workshop
she names first a light fibre used for shirts worn in the warm season
she describes a second rougher fibre meant for bags and aprons
she says that a short-pile cloth swallows the light and suits jackets made for ceremonies
she points out that a pressed material never frays and spares the trouble of finishing the edges
she buys in narrow strips an openwork cloth that she stitches onto collars
the openwork cloth costs the most because it calls for a patient hand
she holds that the choice of a material follows the purpose of the piece
she says the pupil will know the cloths by touch before knowing them by sight
text: The dressmaker answers her pupil, who wants to know what all the cloth stacked round the workshop is for. Linen comes first, cool and supple, kept back for shirts worn through the warm months. Hemp comes next, coarser under the hand, sturdy enough for bags and aprons. Velvet, she says, swallows the light, and that is why it suits jackets made for ceremonies. Felt never frays, so its edges can be left exactly as they were cut. Last of all she lifts the lace, bought in narrow strips and stitched along collars. Her pupil asks which of them costs the most. The lace, by some way, because it wants a patient hand and an eye trained on fine work. What settles the choice, she adds, is what the piece has to do, never taste on its own; and before long her pupil will know each cloth by touch before knowing it by sight.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old cloth came from fibres drawn out of plant stems
preparing those fibres called for a soaking and then a beating
getting enough cloth to dress a single chest took several weeks
harnessing a wheel to the distaff raised what could be produced
treadle looms set the weaver's hands free
the steam engine then made the workshops larger
the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could own two
fibres born of chemistry are the most recent step
these recent fibres dry quickly and hardly crease
text: Picture a workshop where thread is still drawn out by hand, wisp by wisp, and you are holding the start of this story. The oldest cloth began in plant stems. The fibres were soaked until they loosened their grip on the stalk, then beaten, then combed out straight, and whole weeks went by before there was enough to dress a single chest. Then some quick mind harnessed a wheel to the distaff, and what came off the spindle climbed sharply. Treadle looms followed, and the weaver's hands were freed for the shuttle alone. Steam took over later, the workshops swelled into something far larger, and the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could keep two of them. The latest turn you are very likely wearing at this moment: threads born of chemistry, quick to dry and stubborn about creasing.

units: the wearing out of a shoe follows mechanical causes
the foot rolls its weight from the back towards the front
this way of bearing down wears the heel first and then the toe
the thinning of the outer layer takes away the cushioning
the unabsorbed shock travels up towards the knee joint
hard surfaces speed up the breaking down of the sole
a sole soaked with water loses its shape and its stiffness
makers stack layers of unequal density
the writer concludes that the stride wears the shoe out more than the material does
text: A shoe does not wear out at random, and the reason is far more mechanical than most people suppose. The foot rolls its weight from the back towards the front, so the sole meets an uneven rub: the heel goes first, the toe follows. Once the outer layer thins, the cushioning is gone and the shock travels up towards the knee joint, which is why keen walkers ache. Hard surfaces hurry the whole thing along, since nothing gives back what it takes in. Wet weather adds its share. A sole that has drunk up water loses its shape, loses its stiffness, and lets the foot slide about inside. Makers answer by stacking layers of unequal density, firm below and yielding above. The shoe holds up far better that way, yet the principle stands: it is the stride that wears a shoe out, not the material.

units: a tear spoils the front of a borrowed dress
the dress has to be given back the next day
a seam sewn edge to edge would have left a visible mark on the satin
the idea of hiding the tear under a belt is dropped
a neighbour who once kept a haberdashery looks the cloth over
the neighbour suggests adding an embroidered motif instead of mending
the embroidered motif shows a stem and three leaves
the owner of the dress notices the motif and asks where it was bought
text: A tear as wide as a fingernail ran across the front of the borrowed dress, and the woman who was due to give it back the following day felt her throat tighten. Sewn edge to edge, the split would have left a visible pucker in the pale satin. She thought of hiding it under a belt, then let the idea go, since the waist of the dress sat far too high. Her neighbour, who had kept a haberdashery years before, turned the cloth towards the window and studied it. She proposed not to mend but to add: pale thread, a stem and three leaves, worked exactly over the wound in the satin. The job filled a whole evening, the needle moving without hurry. The next morning the owner of the dress stopped short in front of the motif and asked where it had been bought. The other said it was not for sale.

units: the choice of a fastening follows the use the piece is meant for
the cord runs through metal rings and spreads the pull over the whole height
the cord can be set finely and replaced for next to nothing
the cord asks for slow handling and works loose when the knot is badly pulled up
the metal fastener closes in one movement and holds without being watched
the metal fastener forces a fixed width that does not follow changes of measurement
lacing is advised for a work garment worn over layers of varying thickness
the metal fastener is advised for a formal jacket because it stays discreet
the edge has to be strengthened against tearing before the assembly
text: Before you settle on lacing or on a hooked fastening, think about what the garment is meant to do. A cord runs through metal rings and spreads the pull over the whole height; you can set it as finely as you like, and replacing it costs next to nothing. Against that, it wants slow hands, and it works loose the moment a knot is badly pulled up. A hook closes in one movement and holds without being watched, though it forces a fixed width on you: let the measurement shift, and the garment will not follow. For a work garment, take the lacing, because the pull has to answer the thickness of whatever is worn beneath. For a formal jacket, the hook keeps quiet and leaves the front undistorted. Either way, make sure the edge is strengthened against tearing before you put the lining in.

units: a trade gathering given over to cloth has just closed
the organisers hold on to four announcements
a group of workshops claims it can pull cutting scraps back into fibre and work them into fresh yarn
a woven label will give the origin of the fibre and the place of dyeing
several retailers undertake to publish the list of their subcontractors
a machine now cuts the woven edge without burning it
this cut does away with the hard ridge that seamstresses had to take off
the exhibitors are waiting for these undertakings to turn into firm orders
text: A trade gathering given over to cloth closed last night, and its organisers hold on to four announcements. The first is about recycling: a group of workshops says it can pull cutting scraps back into fibre and work them into fresh yarn without weakening it. The second is about tracing, since every piece will carry a woven label giving the origin of the fibre and the place where it was dyed. The third touches how the goods are made, several retailers having undertaken to publish the list of their subcontractors. The fourth drew less notice, though the technical people seized on it: a machine now cuts the woven edge without burning it, which does away with the hard ridge that seamstresses used to take off by hand. The exhibitors are waiting to see these undertakings turn into firm orders.

units: a coat hanging near the entrance changes its look as the seasons go by
at the end of the cold season the velvet collar carries the mark of the scarf
the pile of the collar stays flattened one way
through the mild season the garment is brushed and then put away in a cotton bag
the cotton bag lets it lose its smell of smoke
during the hot spell it sleeps folded on a high shelf
it is folded with the lining outwards so as to avoid marks
a damp cloth and a warm iron take out the crease that has appeared across the back
the felt hat keeps a dent for good once the dent is pressed into it
text: The coat hangs on a hook near the entrance, and its look shifts as the seasons go by. At the close of the cold months the velvet collar still carries the mark of the scarf that pressed on it: the pile lies flattened one way and refuses to stand up again. Then the mild weather arrives, the coat is brushed and aired and then hung away in a cotton bag, where it gives up its smell of smoke. Through the hot spell it sleeps on a high shelf, folded in two, the lining turned outwards so that nothing marks the face of the cloth. When the chill comes round again it is brought out with a sharp crease right across the back, which a damp cloth and a warm iron will eventually take out. The felt hat above it goes round the same cycle, but forgives less: press a dent into it and the dent stays.

units: the writer is exasperated by how fragile mass-produced clothes are
the seams give way at the second wash and the linings split
the buyer buys again the garment he has only just worn out
the labels have worked out that quick replacement pays better than strength
makers cut the weight of the cloth and drop the reinforcements at the points of strain
an alteration workshop now turns down certain repairs for want of solid material
the writer notes that customers accept a shirt lasting a single season
the writer believes the change will come from the piled-up cost of bad buys
text: Honestly, the state of mass-produced clothing is enough to try anyone's patience. Seams give way at the second wash, linings split, and the buyer ends up buying again the jacket he has only just worn out. There is nothing mysterious behind it: the labels have worked out that quick replacement pays better than strength. So the weight of the cloth is cut, a thin fibre goes in where linen thread used to be, and the reinforcements at the points of strain quietly disappear. The alteration workshop down the road now turns certain jobs away, because there is nothing solid left for a needle to grip. And we adjust: a shirt lasting a single season strikes us as normal. My own view is that the turn will come from the purse, once the bad buys added together cost more than one garment sewn to last.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a craftsman cuts soles in a narrow room that opens onto the street
he has followed this trade since he left school
customers were bringing things to be mended less and less often
the leather suppliers set batches too heavy for a single workshop
the apprenticeship no longer drew any candidates
he gave up the idea of closing and changed what he does
he now makes wooden lasts to measure for difficult feet
his orders come from doctors and from people who work in rehabilitation
he has trained two apprentices, one of whom already puts the uppers together on her own
he holds that the shape of the foot rules the model and not the other way round
text: In a narrow room that opens straight onto the street, the bootmaker has been cutting soles since the day he left school. His trade very nearly went out with him. Customers were bringing things to be mended less and less often, the leather suppliers set batches too heavy for one workshop to take, and the apprenticeship drew nobody at all. He could have closed. Instead he changed what he does: rather than wait for repairs, he now makes wooden lasts to measure for difficult feet, the ones that mass production rubs raw. His orders come from doctors and from people who work in rehabilitation. He has trained two apprentices, and one of them already puts the uppers together on her own. Asked what he is proud of, he points to a pair on the bench, its sole marked by an uneven tread, and says the foot rules, never the model.

units: two dresses are shown facing each other in a room
the first dress is cut from a dark velvet
the velvet swallows the light and hangs straight
the second dress is of unbleached lace and lets both air and eye through
the wall can be made out behind the openwork dress
the onlooker prefers the dark dress at first because of its bulk
the judgement turns round once the eye lingers
the openwork dress lays out its own drawing, in which each loop holds the next
the onlooker ends up admiring the hand that carried out the work
the heavy piece is forgotten on the way out while the light one keeps pulling the eye back
text: Two dresses face each other in the far room, and nothing about them agrees. The first, cut from a dark velvet, swallows the light; it weighs, it hangs straight, it puts a hush on everything near it. The second, in unbleached lace, lets both air and eye pass through, so that the wall shows behind it, as though the cloth were hesitating to exist at all. At first the comparison goes to the velvet, whose bulk simply commands the room. Then the eye lingers, and the balance tips the other way. Velvet offers a surface and no more, while the lace lays out its own drawing, each loop holding the next with no visible knot. In the end you admire the hand that tied it rather than the dress itself. You leave with an odd impression: the heavier piece slips your mind, the lighter one keeps pulling your eye back.
